title: stability-sweep-stochastic-quant-failure-modes-feb2026
content:
Context and motivation:
This is a working notes doc for a different angle than the usual quant-bench sweeps: instead of sweeping mean accuracy/latency tradeoffs we looked for stochastic failure modes that manifest only under realistic serving dynamics (KV cache reuse, microbatching, asynchronous warmups, and kernel-specific non-determinism). Goal: catalog failure modes, produce a reproducible harness, and propose mitigations we can add to the runtime (deterministic kernels, lightweight drift detection, fallback heuristics).

High-level summary of findings (quick bullets):
- Determinism gaps: AWQ kernels with tiled vector lanes produced non-deterministic low-probability token sequences when run with asynchronous multi-stream execution on A100s (CUDA streams + preemption). Differences are tiny on average (KL vs FP32 < 0.002) but concentrated on tail examples and amplified under repeated prefix reuse.
- Cache amplification: prefix/KV cache reuse magnifies small per-token logprob drifts into measurable output divergence across 10–30 tokens — observed as increased repetition and occasional token collapse.
- Mixed-batch jitter: dynamic batching with mixed-seq-lengths changes kernel control flow and memory alignment; some FP8 kernels show higher p99 token latency variance and occasional throughput regression at high concurrency.
- Failure modes are workload-dependent: instruction-like prompts (code, math) were more robust; high-entropy creative prompts showed higher instability and hallucination spikes when using aggressive quantization (AWQ 4-bit + custom kernel).
- Regression signal: perceptual quality regressions were often not captured by raw perplexity or average logprob; better signals included token-level KL-scores distribution tails, repetition counts, and a simple ‘semantic divergence’ metric (embedding cosine drift of continuation vs FP32).

Experimental design (repro harness notes):
- Models: Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B (community variant), and a 34B-internal test model. For Llama MMLU-type evaluation we used the 13B variant; creative prompts used a 500-prompt creative set we author-curated to stress high-entropy behaviour.
- Quant methods: INT8 (symmetric per-channel), GPTQ (per-layer s8/gptq script), AWQ-4bit, FP8 (E4M3) using vendor kernels.
- Kernels tested: baseline dense GEMM (reference), vectorized-tiling (custom), packed-block (low-memory), CUDA-FP8-optimized, and the AWQ-specific tiled kernel (labelled awq-tile-v2).
- Serving config: A100s (80GB) and H100 small cluster for cross-hardware validation. Runtime flags: async-kernel=true, preemptible-streams=true, dynamic-batching with batch_max_tokens=4096, kv-cache-warmth=warm and cold modes.
- Evaluation metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec throughput under constant-concurrency client, mean token logprob delta vs FP32, KL divergence over next-token distributions (aggregated), repetition-rate (n-gram overlap in continuation), embedding-drift (cosine distance between continuations under quant vs FP32 using a frozen embedding model), and an internal hallucination checklist (binary flags for factual errors on a small fact-check set).

Representative experiment (one we can reproduce quickly):
- Select 50 high-entropy prompts from creative set. Run each prompt 20× with different client interleaving seeds under two modes: cold (clear KV cache per request) and warm (reuse KV cache across a 4-prompt prefix chain). For each kernel/quant method capture token-by-token logprobs and continuations.
- Observed behaviour: AWQ-4bit + awq-tile-v2 on A100 (async-kernel) shows a 0.4% higher repetition-rate and 3× higher variance in token-level logprob tail vs FP32. Under warm cache chains repetition compounds and ~6% of runs produce an outlier catastrophic repetition collapse (same token repeated until max_tokens).

Hypotheses about root causes: (work in progress)
1) Reduced dynamic range + lane-packing rounding in AWQ combined with out-of-order execution yields divergent intermediate activations; small rounding pushes softmax into a different regime for near-uniform distributions (high-entropy prompts).
2) KV cache reuse amplifies divergence because small early-token differences shift attention context and affect subsequent token distribution multiplicatively.
3) Dynamic batching causes kernel code paths with different vector alignment and memory prefetch behavior; FP8 kernels more sensitive to alignment shifts.

Quick stats snapshot (example numbers, averaged):
- p95 latency: FP32 baseline 85ms, INT8 78ms, AWQ-4bit (awq-tile-v2) 72ms but p99 jitter +28% vs FP32 under async loads.
- tokens/sec raw throughput (steady-state): FP32 420 tps, INT8 510 tps, AWQ-4bit 680 tps (best-case), but effective throughput decreases by 7–12% on workloads with many high-entropy prompts due to repeated regeneration fallback events.
- embedding-drift mean cosine: INT8 0.007, GPTQ 0.012, AWQ-4bit 0.035 (tail mass matters more than mean).

Small reproducible example to expose failure locally:
- Use the attached harness (PR referenced in linked_artifacts). Run: python repro_harness.py --model llama-13b --quant awq-4bit --kernel awq-tile-v2 --warm-cache --prompt-file creative-50.txt --repeats 20 --async. Check token logs for runs where repetition-rate > 0.5 (i.e., >50% of tokens are repeated sequences).

Potential mitigations (ordered by implementation cost):
- Short-term: runtime detection and fallback: compute a tiny online KL-tail estimate after first 8 tokens; if tail mass exceeds threshold, switch to an alternative kernel or FP32/INT8 fallback for that request. Fast to implement and low risk.
- Medium-term: deterministic kernel mode: expose deterministic kernels (single-stream, no async preemption) as an opt-in for critical workloads; provide a cost/latency doc explaining tradeoffs.
- Long-term: calibration layers and range-smoothing for AWQ packing that reduce sensitivity to alignment; work with quant authors to add stability constraints into quant step (minimize tail-KL as objective).

Open questions and next steps:
- How much of the instability is hardware-specific? H100 vs A100 comparison shows the same qualitative failure modes but different frequency; we need to quantify per-hardware.
- Can we design a cheap continuous metric to surface these regressions in the Console without running full evals? Proposal: token-tail-KL + embedding-drift rolling window per route/model.
- Tests to add to CI: deterministic reproduction harness (single seed + no async) plus a stochastic harness that runs small randomized prefixes to catch rare catastrophic events.

Notes for docs/console integration:
- Console should surface a new alert type: "quant-stability" with examples, p95/p99 stability score, and a button to force-model fallback per route.
- Add an opt-in route-level flag in API: stability_level={best_effort, stable, deterministic} that maps to kernel and runtime flags.

Appendix: quick checklist for repeating experiments locally
1) Checkout PR linked_artifacts PR/2145 and run container: scripts/dev-start.sh repro-quant-sweep
2) Place creative-50.txt in ./inputs and run repro_harness.py (args in reproducible example above)
3) Inspect token logs in ./outputs/<run-id>/tokens.log for KL and repetition heuristics
4) If you find a catastrophic-run, attach the run-id + tokens.log to CON-3421 for triage.

Working assumptions and caveats:
- This is an early-stage doc: mostly experimental notes and partial numbers. Numbers above are aggregated examples to convey magnitude, not final thresholds to ship.
- We are prioritizing reproducibility; please prefer the repro harness over ad-hoc runs when trying to confirm behaviors.

Questions for the team:
- Maria: can you validate whether the awq-tile-v2 kernel has any non-deterministic code paths when compiled with our current driver flags?
- Liam: can you reproduce the warm-cache amplification on H100 (I suspect different stream preemption behavior changes frequency)?
- Research: any quick ideas for adding a stability loss during quantization to penalize tail-KL without blowing model quality?

Sidenote (notes to self): stash intermediate logs and attach a short sample transcript to the Console example so PMs can see the user-visible difference.

End of doc.
